objective: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practised and developed the sub-skills of reading for gist and detailed comprehension in the context of an introduction to The Outsiders by S.E. Hinton.
materials:
- The Outsiders by S.E. Hinton (Chapter 1)
- YouTube trailer: The Outsiders - Official Trailer (Warner Bros.) — https://youtu.be/uxVZcju_UV0
- Chapter 1 PDF (includes 3 reflection questions at end)

stages.stage_aim: To activate learners' interest in the theme of The Outsiders and build anticipation for the novel
stages.procedure:
- Show the Warner Bros. trailer for The Outsiders (~2 min).
- Elicit initial reactions: 'What do you think this story is about? Who are these people?'
- Pair discussion: 'What does it mean to be an outsider? Can you think of a time you felt like one?'
- Brief class feedback: 'Do you think being an outsider was different in the 1960s than it is today?'

stages.stage_aim: To give learners context about the author and the novel's significance in YA literature
stages.procedure:
- Present S.E. Hinton: Susan Eloise Hinton, born 1948 in Tulsa, Oklahoma.
- Key fact: She wrote The Outsiders at age 15-16 while still in high school and published it at 19 in 1967.
- She is credited with inventing the YA genre — she wanted to write honest, realistic stories about teenagers.
- Pre-teach selected vocabulary: greaser, Socs, reckon, savvy, souped-up (brief board presentation with context from the chapter).
- Show composite cast image.

stages.stage: Setting the Purpose — Why Read Aloud?
stages.stage_aim: To establish the rationale for extensive reading and the reading circle format
stages.procedure:
- Elicit: 'Why do we read out loud together in a reading circle?'
- Highlight benefits: improves fluency, builds vocabulary through context, creates a shared experience, helps hear the natural rhythm of English.
- Explain the lesson format: 20 min guided read-aloud, followed by private reading with reflection questions.

stages.stage_aim: To guide learners through the opening of the novel, focusing on narrative voice, setting, and character introductions
stages.procedure:
- Teacher and students take turns reading Chapter 1 aloud — each student reads a paragraph or two before passing to the next.
- Pause after the Soc attack scene to check comprehension: 'What just happened to Ponyboy? How is he feeling?'
- As each character is introduced (Darry, Sodapop, Steve, Two-Bit, Dally, Johnny), pause briefly to note key traits.
- Draw attention to Ponyboy's narrative voice and his perspective on being a greaser.

stages.stage_aim: To give learners time to absorb the text individually and respond personally through written reflection
stages.procedure:
- Students re-read the chapter silently or continue from where the read-aloud stopped.
- Hand out reflection questions. Students write answers for themselves — this is not assessed, just a way to think about the text.
- If time permits, invite 1-2 students to share one thing they wrote with the class.

reflection_questions: 1. Ponyboy says the greasers are like a family. What makes a group of friends feel like family to you?
2. Darry is hard on Ponyboy, but Sodapop is gentle. Why do you think Darry acts this way?
notes:
The Outsiders is one of the most successful and influential young adult novels ever published. Written by S.E. Hinton at age 15 and published in 1967, it has sold over 15 million copies worldwide, was adapted into a major motion picture directed by Francis Ford Coppola in 1983, and is credited with launching the YA genre as we know it. It remains one of the most widely taught novels in secondary schools.

Reading aloud in a reading circle is grounded in extensive reading pedagogy. Taking turns reading aloud ensures every student remains engaged and accountable — listeners follow the text knowing their turn is coming, which builds anticipation and focus. Hearing fluent pronunciation and rhythm while seeing the words reinforces both auditory and visual processing. The shared experience of reading together lowers the affective filter: students are not performing for a grade but contributing to a collective act of meaning-making. This approach is particularly effective for B1 learners, who benefit from scaffolded access to authentic literary texts. The follow-up reflection questions are deliberately open-ended and ungraded — this promotes genuine personal response to literature rather than a hunt for correct answers, encouraging students to develop their own interpretive voice.
